item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外观察：Leopold 的"OOMs 思维"恰恰是他爆仓的元凶

大多数分析都在说"杠杆害人"，但真正的深层讽刺被所有人忽略了：Leopold 用来预测 AI 未来的思维框架（指数级 OOMs，数量级跃迁），正是他管理风险时的致命盲区。

他的 Situational Awareness 论文教人们"用指数思考"——算力 10x、算法 10x、Unhobbling 10x，复利下去就是 1000x。这套心智模型让他把 2 亿做到 200 亿。但杠杆的可怕之处恰恰在于——它也是指数的，只是方向相反。3.5 倍杠杆下，25% 的下跌被放大成 87.5% 的账户蒸发，这不是线性风险，这是反向 OOM。

一个能看清 AI 指数曲线的人，却看不见杠杆的指数陷阱——这不是智力问题，这是"预测指数"和"承受指数"是两个完全不同的认知肌肉。前者是分析师的脑，后者是外科医生的手。

二、跨领域连接：南韩爆仓 × 果蝇的 64 维大脑 × 芯片崩盘 = 同一个系统性真相

这一集的三条主线看似风马牛不相及，其实指向同一个隐藏结构——当系统的实际维度远超观察者的心智维度时，就会周期性发生"降维崩溃"。

  • 南韩 120 万个杠杆账户被平仓：投资者用 3 维直觉（涨/跌/杠杆倍数）参与了一个至少 10 维的市场（利率、汇率、地缘、AI 叙事、开源冲击、政策、流动性、外资净流入…）
  • 芯片股一周蒸发 1 万亿美元：华尔街把 AI 简化成"NVIDIA + HBM + CoWoS"三个变量，忽略了中国光刻机、开源模型、能源约束等隐形维度
  • 果蝇的 13.9 万神经元需要 64 维空间才能建模：连 3D 欧氏几何都装不下一只果蝇的意识，但人类却用一维（Y/N）判断"AI 是不是泡沫"

啊哈时刻：Freeberg 讲的双曲空间和 64 维神经拓扑，其实就是这集所有金融事件的隐喻——杠杆爆仓的本质，是用低维模型强行套嵌高维现实的必然结果。SBF 破产、Leopold 爆仓、南韩散户被扫，都是同一个"维度错配"故事的不同变体。

三、被忽视的反常识：Anthropic/OpenAI 的"减速呼吁"其实是"复利防火墙"

Sacks 列了五个动机（虚荣、CYA、监管俘获、群体宗教、垄断伪装），全都对，但少了最关键的第六条——时间不对称套利。

前沿实验室现在的收入以 10x/年增长，而算力供给只能 3x/年增长。这意味着一件所有人都没说破的事："减速"对领先者是净收益，对追赶者是净损失。领先者已经占据了最好的算力合约、最贵的数据、最贵的人才，他们需要的只是冻结时间——让追赶者在监管等待期里消耗自己的现金流，而自己继续用垄断利润复利。

这和 19 世纪末洛克菲勒推动的"反托拉斯前的联邦监管"是同一套剧本：当你已经赢了，你就把梯子拉上来，然后呼吁大家"负责任地不再爬梯子"。

更精妙的是——Dario 呼吁的"FDA for AI"和 Mamdani 的"社会主义超市"，本质是同一种权力形态：都通过"为你好"的普世叙事，把选择权集中到极少数决策者手里。一个在旧金山用算法，一个在纽约用面包。全世界正在同时经历一场"善意集权"的文艺复兴——AI 前沿实验室和民主社会主义者在意识形态谱系的两端，却在治理逻辑上惊人同构。

这才是这一集最深的暗线：监管俘获的技术版本和民粹补贴的政治版本，都是"多层次营销式集权"（Freeberg 语），只不过前者卖的是安全，后者卖的是便宜。

📝 转录文本

开场与自嘲

All right, everybody, welcome back. Welcome back to the number one podcast in the world. The core for fantastic for the original quartet is here. Did we peek at like, number two, or number three last week? Is that what happened? I think it was number four in the world. So yeah, usually we're number one in the world. US trending. US trending. We're usually number one globally, but yeah, and sometimes number four US.

I forgot my Starlink, so let me apologize to everybody. That was a critical error when you're on the road or on the water, but you know, it'll be fine. I had five huge leads come in this week. The Glenn Gary, Glenn Ross, enterprise leads. Enterprise sales is a bear because it's super chunky, but the deals are ginormous. So actually got any advice for tomorrow from your enterprise sales days, you close some of those big seven figure deals when you were doing Yammer.

No leverage. Don't put on leverage. No leverage will be taken. That's the name of the show today. Leverage equals risk of ruin. PSA, no leverage. I have the situational awareness to not lever up. That's good. Yeah, you want that situational awareness. I mean, it's kind of out there. I mean, if you name your fund situational awareness, that's... Yeah, come on the pod anytime Leopold.

Leopold Aschenbrenner 爆仓事件

All right, everybody, we got to talk about chip stocks crashing after an all time run up and we had a major hedge fund get margin called and some incredible margin calls happening in South Korea. Leopold Aschenbrenner is a 25 year old hedge fund manager. He left OpenAI two years ago to start his own fund. And apparently, according to reports, this is breaking news on Thursday when we tape, he got margin called and had to sell his entire public portfolio to cover massive losses caused by his leverage.

And who bought them? None other than Citadel's Ken Griffin. We don't know if it was Ken Griffin himself, but Citadel bought it according to the early reports. Leopold had insane returns and he rode the wave of AI and chips and frontier labs as recently as this month. And he started the fund with but $225 million in 2024. He grew it 100x to 20 billion this year or so, ran it all the way up to 45 billion. Now he's at 200x earlier this month by trading on leverage according to our friends at CNBC at the end of the June, who's reportedly up 4x, 450% this year. Some have reported that he's also selling his massive entropic stake to cover these losses. But the Wall Street Journal is disputing it again. We're happy to have him here on the program.

芯片股崩盘全景

How did this all blow up? Well, Nasdaq's chip index — this is called the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index — is down over 20% over the last month. That's bear market territory. Obviously, definition of bear market territory for those of you who don't play in the markets is anything over 20%.

The index included the top 30 US listed chips. That's people like Nvidia, TSMC, AMD, Micron, you know, all those big names. But the index bounce back a bit today up 7% when we're taping. So we may have found a bottom.

Unfortunately for Leopold, he had already sold Samsung and SK Hynix, two South Korean chip companies that are not included in the NASDAQ index. Also got smashed, crushed, demolished. Samsung down 38% over last month. SK Hynix down 14% since going public three weeks ago. The Kospi, that's South Korea's version of the S&P 500, is down over 40% in the last 40 days. Between last Friday and Wednesday, leading chip companies shed over a trillion dollars in market cap combined.

So to put this in context, chip stocks had a legendary run the past couple of years, but trading on leverage, and we'll talk about it, very dangerous. If there's a downturn, we'll get into the South Korea wrinkle as well. Even with this downturn, the five-year results are still spectacular. Tramath Micron up 850%, mostly in the last year. NVIDIA up 875% in the last five years, and Broadcom up 663%.

Chamath 论杠杆的机制

Let's discuss it. If I was going to give you one piece of advice when you're running risk is you have to manage leverage incredibly carefully because when it runs ahead of you, the unwind is incredibly violent and it's incredibly quick. That's the biggest problem with running either massively levered long or massively levered short.

So I don't know to what extent he was running levered, but the rumors are he was running like three and a half turns, which just to give you a sense, when you're running that much risk, a three and 4% move is amplified 12 and 13. But if you saw what's happened in the last three days, a 25% move is amplified 75%. So it has the risk to stop you out. And what happens is when you get that leverage, the banks are given the authority to close you out. And when they close you out, what they do is they start calling around and unwind your risk, and you don't have much of a choice. It's sort of an automatic one-way ratchet.

So if everything that has been reported is accurate, he was running about three and a half times levered, the market moved against him, he lost a very large percentage of his gains. And then the prime brokers started calling folks, Citadel bought the whole book. And now the question is, what is the AUM left and what is the high watermark? And can he actually dig his way out? These things are brutal.

Sacks 论基本面 vs. 动量

Your thoughts, Sax, looking at this situation, any lessons for you? Or I guess, bigger picture, this downdraft, is it because of market conditions, inflation, the war, or people just ahead of their skis when it comes to the valuation of these companies and then he just got caught in a down draft?

Yeah well, I think that is the key question here is this correction in the markets — is it driven by fundamentals or is it driven by momentum? And my view is that I think it's driven by momentum, meaning that over the past year you've had this roughly 10x run up in memory chip stocks. And you've seen this overall huge rise in any stock that's related to the AI boom. So anything related to this AI capex boom has been going up like crazy.

And I think it was inevitable that you'd see a pullback. I think there was something like a 10% pullback in the NASDAQ from the peak, but when you look at this momentum trade it was down like 30 or 40, right? Because the 10 was on the whole market, so this sort of momentum trade was the most exposed part of it. And you look at what happened in South Korea, you look at what happened with Leopold's fund, and obviously there was a lot of leverage behind this momentum trade so when it corrects it's going to be brutal.

But I think that the question again is, does this reveal anything about the fundamentals? And my sense is that you're already seeing the rebound this morning. And what I mean by that when I say fundamentals is, is the CapEx that's being invested in the AI boom, is that real or is it misguided? Is that a sound investment? Is that an investment that the hyperscalers for example should be making? Is that an investment that's eventually going to deliver ROI or is this some sort of bubble? And my view is that it's real, that I think there will be a return on all of this capex.

I don't try to predict stocks or tell people when they should be buyers. But you look at the hyperscalers, they have invested pretty much all of their free cash flow and then some in this boom. A lot of people are trading those stocks down because of that. My view is that eventually there will be a return on that investment. And this is sort of temporary market volatility amplified by leverage.

And Chamath is right. I think it was Warren Buffett or maybe Munger who said that leverage is the only way that smart people go broke. Because if you're not using leverage, your portfolio would just be down 30% this month. And then it would already be up 7% today. So you'd be rebounding. So you'd be down, okay, 20 something percent this month, but after having risen 10X in the past year. But if you're leveraged three or four X, you're wiped out and you get margin called. So look, there's many examples of really smart people getting hurt by leverage. And that's the lesson there.

Leopold 的 "Situational Awareness" 思维框架

Now, I think Leopold's a really interesting figure in the whole AI movement. And I would say an interesting thinker. I met him about a year, year and a half ago.

Did you invest in the fund? Did you give you an opportunity? No, I wasn't an investor. I was prohibited from investing in things like that. Oh, right. You were in DC at the time. Right.

But I thought he was a really interesting thinker. And he wrote a blog called Situational Awareness before he created the hedge fund version of it. And I thought what was really interesting about it was just he laid out the bull case for the AI boom. And just by the way, he's like very wired into Anthropic. I think his fiance is Dario's chief of staff, something like that. You could almost say that he's like the hedge fund version of the Anthropic thesis.

And what I thought was interesting about his argument is he talked about OOMs or orders of magnitude, which he called OOMs, increases in three key areas. So he said that if you look at the raw compute, the chips, they were getting better at a rate of roughly 3x per year, which is roughly an order of magnitude or 10x every two years. He said if you look at the algorithmic efficiency, so techniques like reinforcement learning, things like that, the models were getting better at 3x every year, which is, again, order of magnitude 10x every two years. And then he also said that there were huge gains from what he called unhobbling, which I think now we would look at things like the harness and connectors, you know, ways of using the model. Those are also getting better — the ways of integrating the model's decision making in practical ways that the intelligence actually becomes useful. And he said that that was also similarly improving.

And so you project forward when you have 10x orders of magnitude improvement in these key underlying fundamentals, these key drivers of the technology. You can see that well over a course of not just two years, but over four years, you're going to have 100x improvement, over six years, you're going to have 1000x improvement, right? Because it's — yes, and you rarely see anything in the world that grows at that velocity, we'd be hard pressed here, with the exception of maybe bandwidth, you know, going to 5G or to the home or something like, what's an analogy where that's happened before in history?

Virality, I mean, you know, back in the PayPal days with the PayPal mafia, we would think in this way, of exponential increases because we would see an exponential growth curve. And so we were able to project forward. So his thinking in OOMs always appealed to me because I think most people just don't think in exponentials or don't know how to think in exponentials. It's hard for humans to think in exponentials, right? When numbers get big, it's like the difference between a billion and a trillion is a lot. It's not a small amount. Yeah.

And you'd have to say, look, he was stunningly successful for the first couple of years. Apparently he started with 200 million or so in his hedge fund. and he rolled that all the way up to 20 billion, I think. Now, the problem, I mean, the reason why I think he got wiped out, or at least his public book did, is it's partly the leverage, and then you have the short-term volatility. So those two things don't go together. Also, when your fund grows that much, you get a lot of hot money. So when you say, well, he's up 10x before the 30% correction, well, the question is, who's up 10x? Obviously, the investors who were there from the beginning are up 10x or more, but the latest people, that's only 200 million, right? So if 10 billions come in in the last few months because of the hot money dynamic where everyone piles into the most successful head funds, those guys are kind of wiped out.

Freeberg 论心理与 SBF 类比

So let's talk about the psychology of this, Dave Freberg. If somebody is so brilliant that they can write this essay and understand the market so exquisitely and be such a great communicator? How could they have such a crazy blind spot when it comes to putting on leverage at this scale? Do you have any thoughts on that, Friedberg? Have you seen it before? Is it just the folly of using... It's not a blind spot. It's a feature that turns into a bug. We're all like this. We all know people that have that edge and can push it.

What do you think, Friedberg, on the personality type or is this just something most people do when they're on the heater? Conviction. Where do you stand on it? Ultra conviction.

I think the Warren Buffett assessment of equity markets is in the short term, they're voting machines. In the long term, they're weighing machines. And you could have the right long-term view. I mean, look at SBF. SBF pretty much would have been the greatest investor of all time if he didn't get liquidated. Same dynamic. I mean, obviously there was fraud in terms of how he was allocating capital, but his actual portfolio over the long run was absolutely correct.

In the same way that if you had bet on the internet and stayed in that bet from 1995 through to today, and you bought a portfolio of internet stocks, a bunch of them would have fallen to the wayside. But those that won, 1,000X, 2,000X, 20,000X, and you do extraordinarily well. So he could be right in his fundamental assessment and analysis. But then in markets over the short term, you have bubbles and bubbles pop. And when bubbles pop, if you have a leverage to multiply your returns, you get wiped out. That's effectively you know what's going on here. And he may be right.

南韩 120 万散户大爆仓

You know, the thing to really double click on that I think will probably come out in the next couple of days or weeks is just how historic the South Korea unwind was. 1.2 million leverage trading accounts have been hit with margin calls in South Korea. If you know about the South Korean market, that data is two weeks old, J Cal, that number is much bigger today. Yeah, yeah.

But I mean, just in terms of people discussing it in relation to him getting caught in the downdraft, if anything, he got caught in this downdraft of those 1.2 million levered accounts. Somewhere around 350,000 of them were fully liquidated already. And so two weeks old, that's — so as of today, the number is much bigger, right? It could be closer to a million accounts fully liquidated today. If that's the case, we're talking about like, some percentage of South Korean population, having their entire asset base blown out — their entire percent of the population — and that's gonna sting.

And it is a very investment forward culture. If you look at what happened in crypto, the same thing happened with NFTs and speculation there. And they had banned crypto because they knew the Korean culture has this gamble in it.

Freeberg 的宏观分析：赤字、利率与 AI 的短期矛盾

Can I just frame something up? So if we take the circumstance of there's a good long-term bet in AI that can be made in the markets. But in the short term, there is an exuberance that arises. The question is, what's resetting that exuberance? What's bringing us back down to earth in the short term? And I think if you take a zoom out, there's a bunch of other statistics and other facts on the ground that I think are big macro drivers at the moment.

If you take a look at the 30 year treasury yield, we just crossed 5.2% for the first time in 20 years. So you could buy US treasuries that are paying you 5.2% a year for 30 years, which on a pre-tax equivalent basis, probably 8, 9%, 9% from the US government. For 30 years. So, Nick, if you zoom out, you know, we have not seen this yield on U.S. Treasury since 2007, leading up to the global financial crisis when they cut rates and printed money.

At the same time, there was some probability that the Federal Reserve was going to raise rates this week. They didn't. And that obviously would have tampered the inflation risk ahead of us. Number one is virtue signaling, and that can never be underestimated as a motive in Silicon Valley.

Number two is there's a CYA aspect to this, which is if something terrible happens, they're going to be able to say, well, we wanted to stop. You made us keep going. It's not our fault. It's your fault.

Number three is reg capture. Dario wants an FDA for AI. He's not going to stop until he gets it. And in order to get it, you have to keep spiking the cortisol and panic people. So I think that's a big part.

There was a precedent with Google Books. It was originally codenamed Project Ocean at Google a long time ago. They took all these books and we had this giant facility in Mountain View. And the innovation at the time was a two-dimensional infrared grid projected on the pages because they didn't cut the books. They had a human sitting there flipping the pages. Camera would take picture, built our own OCR software to adjust the book images. And there was kind of ultimately when this product came out, Google Books, you could kind of search through all the books in the world and — and magazines. And access information and later magazines, yeah.

And there was three categories. There was the public domain, which is out of copyright. Then there's the kind of in copyright but out of print. And then there's the in copyright and in print. And there was a class action lawsuit filed in 2005 by the Authors Guild and the Association of American Publishers that disagreed with Google's claim of fair use. And that ended up in a three year negotiation and in court out of court that ended up in a deal where Google would split two thirds, one third of the revenue generated with all these rights holders and for out of copyright books. People could read up to 20% of the text for free and then they would sell this kind of full digital access and that was the deal. But then later a federal judge rejected that deal which was eventually signed in 2008-2009 and the federal judge said no way, send it back, this isn't going to work. Google appealed and in 2015 second circuit court of appeals ruled in Google's favor and the whole thing was settled and they basically declared Google did in fact have fair use under copyright law in the way that they were showing snippets of copyrighted books in the material. Yes, you can't read the entire book like it's a Kindle. You can search the book, find the paragraph. Provide a reference to it, right?

And so the question on fair use in AI is, can my understanding or extraction of value of the knowledge from the data in the book give me the ability to provide better answers to you through the AI chat interface or services that I'm providing you. And I think it's going to be — Tesla. And I think we'll see. I do think fundamentally that the conversion of that data into what I would call knowledge and ultimately the ability to create new outcomes from that knowledge that are not copyrighted, that are not copies of the original material, I do think is going to end up being the right fair use policy and is going to be the right read on fair use. So I think it'll likely get litigated and I think it'll take a couple of years and I'll get kind of, I'm hoping one of these.

Just to be clear, Jake, how I have not changed my view on fair use. So I am with Freeberg on this. My point is the hypocrisy. Yes. They're not checking IDs because IDs are racist and you know you can't check IDs to vote so we shouldn't be able to check IDs for grocery stores. So people will come in from all over the place to use these grocery stores. The demand will go up and then they'll start to open more and more grocery stores like this. And let's say each one loses 10 million a year and they get to 10 or 20 of these — that's $200 million of losses per year on the grocery store chain. But it creates this extraordinary social movement for more of these grocery stores supporting the DSA and so on. $200 million a year on a $125 billion a year budget for the city of New York. It's nothing. It's less than a quarter of a percent of the city's budget. That is so cheap to market the DSA platform and to get the DSA platform to become a social marketing element that drives the next wave here. So again, I do think that these grocery stores, believe it or not, they sound silly, they sound small, but I predict that they will be deemed a point of success and they will end up being a big part of the fuel for the DSA going into 2028.

I couldn't agree with you more. This is gonna play. This will be a great, great feather in their cap. It's gonna be a great example of affordability. Because we've talked about here previously, Trump promised affordability, hasn't been able to deliver it, inflation's up, spending's up, all that great stuff. And Mamdani got it done — free buses, rent controlled, and now you got your discounted grocery store.

Both sides are reacting to the fiscal and monetary condition of the United States. We're overspending, inflation has run away. So you just keep spending more and printing more to give people what they need, which is basic services. And so as the government spends more, then the fundamental cost of those things goes up and you're reducing economic productivity and it becomes a spiraling problem. It is a two-party problem. This is not just one side and the other. Because fundamentally, if you go — I've spent a lot of time now in DC. I think everyone's well intentioned in the White House and the administration in trying to reduce federal spending. But the bigger issue that you face is when you go to Congress and you meet with everyone in Congress, they are representing the interests of their state or of their congressional district. And their objective is to fundamentally drive spending towards their district to give their people more. Their economic incentive and their political incentive is not to give people less, which is what you have to do when you cut programs, when you cut spending.

So the shift in the policy has been, hey, I guess we're not going to be able to cut spending because there's just too much Edwin's in Congress. So the answer is, let's grow through economic productivity gains. And that's the big fuel for AI, the capex depreciation policy and so on. But I think that's been the shift.

So look, I don't know. The one thing I will say critical of President Trump here is when it came to like starting a war, when it came to tariffs, he had no problem like using executive power and telling Congress and everybody in the party, this is the way it's going to be. If you break ranks, I'm going to destroy you. I'm going to get you primaried. And when it comes to spending, you know, it's like, yeah, yeah, you know what? I'm not taking that on. It's too unpopular.

Science Corner: 果蝇大脑与 64 维超几何

All right, Freeberg. The Sultan of Sciences fans have been begging for a science corner. Do you have one this week? They want to know. Do you have something? Oh, Sultan. Oh, Sultan of Science. What can you tell us? Educate us.

Okay, so today I'm going to pull up this paper. Nick, if you can pull it up. A paper. From February of 2026. February. Okay. February. February. February. February. Oh, it's February. Well, what's the problem?

Okay, so this is a group of researchers out of Budapest. Budapest. And there was a really interesting modeling exercise they went through to understand how neurons were connected in the brain, to build a network model, a topological model. And the way they were able to do this is back in October of 2024, there was a group out of Cambridge and Princeton that used electron microscopes to scan the brain of the Drosophila fruit fly. And they mapped every single neuron in that fruit fly's brain — 139,000 neurons. And every connection that the neurons had to other neurons in the brain. So there were 50 million synaptic connections between the neurons.

And it's those connections that make neural networks in the brain work. How are those neurons networked together to do the things that they do? This is the key question in what is that network model? What is the topological model of how neurons connect in the brain, which gives rise to our ability to control our bodies, to seeing things and comprehending vision, comprehending sound, and even the basic premise of consciousness itself. Yes.

So trying to understand the network model for neurons has been this kind of great endeavor of neurobiology forever. This data set was created in October 2024, with just 139,000 neurons. And you know, that's a tiny, tiny, tiny, tiny brain. This would be put it in context versus the human brain — I mean, what are we talking about here? The human brain has on the order of 86 billion neurons. Okay, compared to 50 — And so that means it would be a multiple for the network connections, right? Yes, exactly. On the order of trillions of connections. Okay.

So they took these 50 million connections in the brain and the 139,000 neurons, and then they applied the network model that predicts whether a neuron is connected to another neuron. That's how you're measuring the quality of the model. How correct is it in making a prediction? And when you build the model using what's called Euclidean geometry, so just normal space that we live in, three-dimensional space, they came up with a score and the score was not very good. You couldn't do a great job of just looking at how all the neurons were connected using their physical relationship to each other, how far apart they are to each other in 3D space.

So then they said, well, let's try and model how these neurons are all connected to each other in what's called hyperbolic space. Hyperbolic space is a theoretical type of space, unlike Euclidean geometry, where the further away you get, the wider space gets. So space actually is curved. I know that's a hard concept to describe, but imagine that, you know, as you and I walk farther and farther apart from each other, the area around us actually accelerates in terms of how much space there is, and it expands. It would be space as we know it. Like three-dimensional space as humans understand it when they're on planet Earth. It's a little bit more like space that you would experience in the warping around a gravity well or the warping around a black hole or something like that.

And so in that space, they found that this is where the model was most performative. They were able to map in hyperbolic space how all of these neurons connect to each other. And if you think about it, the further away you get from the first neuron, you're going to have many, many more neurons you can start to tap into. And so hyperbolic modeling on the neuronal connections actually makes sense. And they got a decent score.

And then they went back and they said, well, what if we could use Euclidean geometry, but not in three dimensions, but they went up to four, five, six. And they found that they were able to kind of get as good as the hyperbolic space at 64 dimensions. So by taking normal space and saying, let's use a 64 dimension framework for how we can start to connect all these neurons together, that's where they had the best predictive model.

This is a really interesting kind of discovery. First of all, it can be used for neural network design and AI and other sorts of things. But for me, it highlights the miracle of biology in finding complexity in 64 dimensions, not in three dimensions, but in 64 dimensions, biology found a way to create consciousness, to create vision, to create comprehension, to create control over physical bodies, then to map it and squish it all into a tiny little brain. It did this in effectively 64 dimensions.

It's mind-blowing when you think of it because a fruit fly or a mosquito and, you know, these things, they don't have like a big mission, right? Like their mission is to go find food and procreate. I guess they have a very simple mission too, Jake Cal. Wow. But then we also want to do podcasts and debate politics and philosophy. Don't judge how the mosquito spends their free time.

But yeah, I mean, right, but nobody would argue there's like consciousness as we experience it in a fruit fly. So then you get to trillions — you wouldn't know. But I mean, maybe this is really interesting because it turns out that the biology of how all the neurons are connected, even in a brain as simple as a fruit fly with 50 million connections, is so complex that it has to take 64 dimensions for us to represent how those networks are built, how they're made.

And at 64 dimensions, you could start to argue that perhaps consciousness is a connectivity to a dimensionality that we don't live in every day. You and I don't live in every day. And we can't comprehend. And that it is this extraordinary complexity in 64 dimensions that gives rise to consciousness, that gives rise to our capacity as biological beings to do this very simple thing of thinking.

I just think that it was such a powerful and amazing paper in just bringing forth these numbers and showing just network modeling on this tiny little brain as being just a glimmer into the complexity of how biology has found a path beyond our kind of understanding even of physics into this universe that we can't even comprehend. And it shows how little we know. We know very little.

意识、硅基与生物学

But then as you sort of alluded to here and as we talked about in the top of the show, we have AI frontier labs saying, hey, reinforcement learning is like super dangerous because these things could get out of control. Are you, you know, in the camp of we are rebuilding in this simulation or whatever we're experiencing here we are in fact recreating our brains with silicon? And that, you know, we're on the way to actually creating consciousness that a replicant in science fiction like Blade Runner, where they don't even know, you know, Rachel doesn't know she's a replicant — spoiler alert, you had 50 years to see the film. Like, are you part of that camp that that's actually what's being built here?

Yeah, I'm not sure. It's a longer conversation. We should do it another time. Yeah. But I do think there's something fundamental to consciousness that relates to the drive for survival in a physical sense. You have to have physical sensing and physical responsiveness to learn as a baby, you first start touching hot stuff and cold stuff and you learn. And we build these reward mechanisms into neural networks that we build in AI, but those reward mechanisms are digital and they're programmed. And the question is, is there a reward mechanism that arises in biology that creates a different capacity for consciousness than perhaps can exist in silicon? Bigger topic for a different day with probably people that have spent more time thinking about it than I.

But I just think that there's something about biology. You know, I always tell people this analogy, I've said it many times on the show, I'll say it again. In a single cell, there's 10 billion proteins that work so fast that one second is the equivalent of 80 years of humans walking around the city of Manhattan, never sleeping, doing stuff together with 500 story tall skyscrapers doing stuff for 80 years is one second in one cell. And so you have 10 trillion cells in your body doing that, living that entire universe every second, all interacting with each other. And you start to realize that there's a complexity in what's emerged in biology that extends well beyond any model we built in silicon today. It doesn't mean that the silicon that we're building today doesn't create extraordinary capacity for humanity. But we are very early and the more we kind of understand this sort of thing, like this paper that I just shared, I think the more we realize how little we do know and how much of a frontier there still is to explore.

Yeah, and I think, you know, this obviously brings up faith. And do you believe that there is a God that set this in motion? I like to believe there is some higher work here. And this is my closest analogy in science fiction. We're both super fans of science fiction. But for me, 39 seconds in here, one of the great — I love the Prometheus version of this where there's engineers who are terraforming and started this crazy thing out and there's this experiment in biology going on. And you know, the opening scene here in Prometheus, he drinks this and this is the sacrifice like Jesus sacrificed for humanity and he sacrifices himself here by drinking that biological design, right? And he falls into this, you know, planet Earth, which is just water. And this is the Cambrian explosion where his DNA goes into the river, gets washed out, and then starts the cycle of life on planet Earth. And that these engineers are going around.

It's pretty fantastical. Yeah. A lot of this stuff is a simple way of humans trying to explain stuff, but the complexity that arises in biology, we just can't explain. And I think we try and use these reductive kind of heuristics to try and do it. And it's very, um, you know, it's, it's comforting, because it's so overwhelming, the complexity of how this stuff emerges is too overwhelming. So we create simple stories to try and help ourselves feel better. And yeah, this is my — and that's my favorite story of it is somewhere between Blade Runner and this, by the way, both by the same incredible director. Ridley Scott. So take it for what it's worth.

收尾

All right, everybody. Another amazing episode. You got your science corner. I'll see you next time. Bye-bye. I love you, besties.

Your winner's right. Rain Man, David Sacks. And it said, we open source it to the fans. We just got creative. Love you, besties. I'm a queen of kids. Your winner's right. Besties are gone. We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy because they're all just useless. It's like this like sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. You're a bee. What? You're a bee. We need to get merch. We're lonely.

## 一、意外观察：Leopold 的"OOMs 思维"恰恰是他爆仓的元凶
大多数分析都在说"杠杆害人"，但真正的深层讽刺被所有人忽略了：**Leopold 用来预测 AI 未来的思维框架（指数级 OOMs，数量级跃迁），正是他管理风险时的致命盲区**。
他的 Situational Awareness 论文教人们"用指数思考"——算力 10x、算法 10x、Unhobbling 10x，复利下去就是 1000x。这套心智模型让他把 2 亿做到 200 亿。但杠杆的可怕之处恰恰在于——**它也是指数的，只是方向相反**。3.5 倍杠杆下，25% 的下跌被放大成 87.5% 的账户蒸发，这不是线性风险，这是**反向 OOM**。
一个能看清 AI 指数曲线的人，却看不见杠杆的指数陷阱——这不是智力问题，这是**"预测指数"和"承受指数"是两个完全不同的认知肌肉**。前者是分析师的脑，后者是外科医生的手。
## 二、跨领域连接：南韩爆仓 × 果蝇的 64 维大脑 × 芯片崩盘 = 同一个系统性真相
这一集的三条主线看似风马牛不相及，其实指向同一个隐藏结构——**当系统的实际维度远

item.title: [Lex Clips] What caused the American Civil War? | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"废奴叙事"：这场战争其实是关于"扩张权"的博弈

大多数人对南北战争的想象是：北方要废除奴隶制，南方要保住奴隶制。但 Gallagher 的叙述揭示了一个更精细的真相——1860 年真正撕裂美国的问题并非"存废"，而是"扩张"。共和党的纲领里明确写着"奴隶制在其存在的地方可以继续"，只是不允许它进入联邦领地。

这意味着这场战争本质上是一场关于"未来人口结构"的预判性战争：南方精英算出了一笔账——如果奴隶制不能随疆域西扩，那么自由州将永远在参议院和众议院中占据多数，联邦政府终将被"自由化的多数"所控制。他们不是在保卫今天的奴隶制，他们是在预防未来某一天的废奴投票。

这里出现一个反直觉的洞见：南方发动战争，恰恰是因为他们意识到自己在民主程序中已经必然失败。战争成了输家在还有筹码时的最后一搏。这个逻辑与"修昔底德陷阱"惊人相似——不是崛起者挑战守成者，而是衰落者在自己彻底衰落前抢先掀桌。

二、废奴主义者的悖论：道德最清晰的人，被最广泛地厌恶

Gallagher 提到一个容易被现代听众忽略的事实：废奴主义者在北方也被普遍鄙视，被视为"搅乱联邦、加深裂痕"的"煽动者"。1844 年自由党的最高得票率只有 2.5%。

这里藏着一个跨领域的普遍规律——我称之为"先知税"（Prophet Tax）。历史上，那些道德判断走在系统前面的人，几乎无一例外首先被视为社会稳定的破坏者，而非真理的宣讲者。这在科学史中对应着塞麦尔维斯（推广洗手消毒者被同僚驱逐至疯人院），在企业史中对应着内部举报人（安然、波音的工程师），在技术史中对应着早期警告 AI 风险的研究者。

一个真正让人清醒的观察是：一个社会容忍不义的能力，往往强于它容忍指出不义者的能力。因为不义已经嵌入了系统的"沉没成本"，而指控则暴露了每一个默许者的共谋。北方多数白人并非爱奴隶制，他们只是更爱那个不必面对奴隶制的联邦。

三、辉格党之死：一个"跨区域政党"的网络拓扑崩溃

这是整段访谈中最容易被忽略但结构上最深刻的洞察：辉格党的死亡先于战争。辉格党在南北都有分部，试图在奴隶制议题上保持沉默；民主党做到了（暂时地），辉格党做不到，所以 1852 年后消亡。1860 年民主党也最终分裂成南北两派候选人。

这可以用网络拓扑学来理解：任何跨越"深层价值断层线"的组织都是一种"承重结构"，它靠模糊、妥协、议题回避维持连接。当外部压力增加，最先崩塌的不是极端方，而是中间的桥接节点。辉格党就是那个先断的桥。

跨领域的类比令人不安： - 苏联 1991 年解体，先崩的是能够跨越加盟共和国的全联盟共产党； - 今天的美国民主党/共和党，正在承受类似辉格党当年的压力——试图在气候、移民、身份政治等"深层断层"上同时代表都市与乡村； - 大型跨国公司在文化战争中的沉默策略，本质上是在扮演当年的民主党——用模糊换生存。

当你看到一个组织突然对某个议题极度沉默，它可能正是最后的辉格党。

四、隐藏的洞见：为什么不拥有奴隶的白人也为奴隶制而战？

访谈末尾那个细节值得单独抽出：大多数南方白人家庭并不拥有奴隶，但所有白人都在奴隶制中有"股份"。Gallagher 用了一个精妙的例子——小农没有轧棉机，去富邻居家借用；作为回报，他要轮班参加"奴隶巡逻队"（slave patrol）。

这是一个几乎完美的共谋经济学模型：制度不是靠受益者维系，而是靠互惠性小恩惠+对替代方案的恐惧（海地起义的阴影）编织成一张网。南方白人不需要拥有奴隶，他们拥有的是"不必是最底层"的心理保险。

这个模型解释的东西远远超出 1860 年的南方——它解释了为什么工人阶级会支持削减自己福利的政客（只要那能进一步伤害更底层的人），为什么种姓制度能在印度延续千年，为什么办公室的"隐形等级"比工资等级更难打破。任何持久的不公正制度，本质上都在贩卖一种"你至少不是最下面那个"的心理产品。

一个让人不安的收束：Gallagher 反复强调"废奴与反种族歧视不是一回事"——你可以反对奴隶制却依然种族歧视。这个区分对今天有直接的杀伤力：我们今天反对一件事的理由，未必是那件事本身错的理由。北方反对奴隶制扩张，不是因为爱黑人，而是因为不想被排挤出西部土地。历史的"进步"，常常是两个错误的方向恰好在某一点上重合。

📝 转录文本

The Question: Causes and Inevitability

Lex: The American Civil War broke out in 1861. What were the causes of the Civil War? Could it have been avoided or was it inevitable?

Gary Gallagher: I don't know if anything is inevitable in history, but it's certainly safe to say that the conditions were in place to make it possible. By the winter of 1860–61, the conditions that made it possible were all related to the institution of slavery and its effects — both in the states where slavery was allowed and in the states where it was not allowed. And there had been a series of tensions that grew in the decade preceding — the 1850s.

Not Abolition, but Expansion

It's not that one side wants to get rid of slavery and the other side wants to protect slavery. I'm talking about the white people in the United States now, who would be making the political decisions. It's a question of whether slavery was going to be able to expand into federal territories. That is what really created the starkest difference between the two sections in the 1850s, even in the late 1840s.

The issues that came to the most perilous point, in the view of many people then, had to do with whether slavery would be allowed only where it already existed, or would it be allowed to expand. If it could expand, then it seemed that it might be conceivable at some point even that the slaveholding states could end up with a majority. They were in a minority by 1860–61 and feeling beleaguered, feeling threatened. They'd long since lost the population race to the free states.

Early in the nation, the most powerful states were slaveholding states. Virginia was by far the most important state. Four of the first five presidents were from Virginia — all slaveholders, all prominent members of the slaveholding class. Those days were long gone by the late 1850s.

Lex: So that's an important thing to say. It wasn't, before the Civil War, a discussion about abolishing slavery. It's about whether slavery, the institution of slavery, should be expanded.

Gary Gallagher: Allowed to expand into federal territories.

The Abolitionists: A Despised Minority

There is a portion of the white population that is adamantly in favor of getting rid of slavery immediately — the abolitionists. There was even a political party called the Liberty Party that ran a candidate in 1840, and they got a handful of thousand votes. They reached their high point in 1844 — they got about 2½% of the vote.

The abolitionists are a tiny minority. Even in the North, a tiny minority among the white people of the United States. The African-American population — nearly 4 million of them by 1860 — of course would have embraced it instantly and yearned for it. But in the white population, the abolitionists are a tiny minority. They are much despised even across much of the North, because they were seen as agitators who roiled the Union and deepened rifts that might bring a significant political break.

How It Escalated: The Collapse of the Party Systems

Lex: So how did this escalate to a civil war? This almost policy discussion about institutional slavery — how did it actually escalate?

Gary Gallagher: It escalated into a civil war because in the presidential election of 1860 — there had been two party systems in the United States. The first party system: the Republicans, the Jeffersonian Republicans, versus the Federalists. After that, the two parties were the Whig Party against the Democratic Party. The Democratic Party grew out of the Jeffersonian Republican Party — it's the same party.

The Whig Party was founded to a significant degree on the issue of slavery. How do you maintain a national party that has a wing in the southern states and has a wing in the northern free states that can handle the issue of slavery? The Democrats managed to do that. The Whigs could not do it. And so the Whig Party ran their last significant presidential candidate in 1852.

The Republican Party emerged in the mid-1850s, took most of the old Whigs into the Republican ranks. And one of the key Republican platform planks was: no expansion of slavery into the territories. Not abolish slavery — no expansion. That was the key in 1856 when they ran their first candidate. In 1860, that is again the key plank in the Republican platform. The Republican platform in 1860 says: where slavery exists, it will continue. But it cannot expand into the territories.

When white Southerners saw that, that meant that they were doomed to become an increasingly minority section in the nation. And you would have a federal government increasingly dominated by the free states that could then do the one thing that the white South could not countenance — and that is tamper with the institution of slavery in the South.

The 1860 Election and Secession

The presidential election of 1860 brought the destruction of the last national party, which were the Democrats. They couldn't even settle on a candidate, so you end up with a Northern Democratic candidate running — Stephen A. Douglas. And a Southern candidate running — the convention fractured — and John C. Breckinridge ran on the Southern Democrat platform. You had a Unionist candidate running who just didn't want to talk about slavery — "let's talk about the Union." And you had Lincoln running as a Republican.

When Lincoln won, the white South looked at Lincoln winning — here's a guy who has said that he doesn't think slavery would expand, but he said more than that. He scared the white South more, because in 1858 both Lincoln and William Henry Seward — these are two prominent Republicans — had said, basically in separate speeches (the "House Divided" speech on Lincoln's part, the "Irrepressible Conflict" speech on Seward's part), that the nation could not continue in the long term half slave and half free. And everybody in the South knew which way they wanted it to be. They would want it to be no slavery.

And so Lincoln's election scared the white South enough so that seven of the 15 slaveholding states seceded in response to Lincoln's election. They seceded between December 20th, when South Carolina went out, and the end of February. The Deep South went out.

The View from 1860: Popular Attitudes

Lex: What was the general view amongst the populace towards slavery? Let's lay it out — for the audience looking back, let's put ourselves in the mind space of how people saw the world, how people saw slavery, how people saw African-Americans.

Gary Gallagher: Well, the baseline among white Americans — there were about 31 (shade more than 31) million Americans in 1860 for the census of 1860. About 4 million of them were African-Americans; 3½ million of those enslaved in the South.

Among the white population, the average attitude toward black people is what we would call profoundly prejudiced. A lot of people think this is a Southern white thing — they're the only ones who were prejudiced. By our standards, the overwhelming majority of people in the free states were also deeply prejudiced.

It's important to keep in mind that attitudes toward slavery and attitudes toward race are not necessarily the same. I mean, you could be against slavery and still be prejudiced against black people. By our standards, many abolitionists were prejudiced against black people.

Demographics of the Free States

The overwhelming majority of the white North — I often have a hard time getting my students to understand the demographics in 1860. The free states in 1860 were more than 98% white. African-Americans are a tiny minority in the free states. Black people live in the 15 slaveholding states in 1860.

Most of the white North, by our standards, was very prejudiced. They were against the expansion of slavery into the territories because they thought that would circumscribe white opportunities to make an economic life in these federal territories. And they didn't want that to happen.

About 45% of the people who lived in the free states were Democrats. Most Democrats had no problem with slavery — I mean, absolutely no problem with the institution of slavery. There would be more problems among Republicans, especially with extension of slavery, although many Democrats — white Democrats in the North — were against that as well.

Every White Southerner's Stake in Slavery

The white South was overwhelmingly in favor of slavery. You often read the argument — the kind of neo-Confederate argument — that they'll talk about how most Confederate soldiers didn't own slaves. That's true. A large majority of families in the South did not own a single slave. But all white Southerners had a stake in slavery.

They had a stake in it as a form of labor control, but more important than that, they had a stake in it as a means of social control. They knew — no matter what they said later in the Jim Crow era about how happy black people were in the institution of slavery — they knew that black people, of course, did not want to be enslaved, and they were afraid of what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore.

They had in the backs of their minds Haiti. Is that what's going to…? If you live in one of the coastal districts of South Carolina where 90% of the residents are enslaved, and you're a white person, you probably don't sleep all that soundly at night if you think there's any chance that the black people are not going to remain under the control of the white people.

So all white people in the South had a stake in slavery — not just some, all of them did. And there were all kinds of ways that it would go back and forth. If you were a modest farmer and grew a little bit of cotton, you didn't have your own cotton gin, but your more wealthy neighbor had a gin — he could gin your cotton there, and then you would take your turn on the slave patrol. So there's a reciprocity in that regard.

大多数人对南北战争的想象是：北方要废除奴隶制，南方要保住奴隶制。但 Gallagher 的叙述揭示了一个更精细的真相——1860 年真正撕裂美国的问题并非"存废"，而是"扩张"。共和党的纲领里明确写着"奴隶制在其存在的地方可以继续"，只是不允许它进入联邦领地。
这意味着这场战争本质上是一场**关于"未来人口结构"的预判性战争**：南方精英算出了一笔账——如果奴隶制不能随疆域西扩，那么自由州将永远在参议院和众议院中占据多数，联邦政府终将被"自由化的多数"所控制。他们不是在保卫今天的奴隶制，他们是在预防未来某一天的废奴投票。
这里出现一个反直觉的洞见：**南方发动战争，恰恰是因为他们意识到自己在民主程序中已经必然失败**。战争成了输家在还有筹码时的最后一搏。这个逻辑与"修昔底德陷阱"惊人相似——不是崛起者挑战守成者，而是**衰落者在自己彻底衰落前抢先掀桌**。

💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的悖论：华尔希在"卸下神秘感"，市场却因此更迷茫

大多数人把美联储的"前瞻指引"看作官僚废话，但华尔希这场发布会揭示了一个反直觉的系统悖论：当央行主动放弃"神秘感"、拥抱市场信号时，市场反而恐慌。

为什么？因为前瞻指引本质上是一种"认知外包合同"——市场用降低分析成本换取美联储的确定性承诺。华尔希撕掉了这份合同，说"我们跟你们一样看数据"。听起来民主、透明，但等于把决策的认知负担甩回给市场参与者。而市场厌恶的从来不是坏消息，是分析成本的突然抬升。

这里有一个隐藏的博弈论层次：格林斯潘时代的"迷雾"其实是一种流动性补贴——用信息不对称换取市场的秩序感。华尔希把这个补贴撤了，30年期国债立刻用陡峭化曲线回敬他："你说的话，我不信。"

二、跨领域连接：AI资本开支的"第二局"叙事，与17世纪荷兰东印度公司惊人相似

Gallipo说AI是"九局比赛的第二局"。但这里有一个他没说破、值得警觉的历史回响：所有历史上真正改变文明的资本开支狂潮，都是从"循环融资"开始，以"谁接最后一棒"结束。

看Meta、Microsoft、Oracle互相借贷、互相下订单、互相入股——这个结构不是新的。1602年成立的荷兰东印度公司也是这样：造船商、香料商、阿姆斯特丹银行家们互相持股、互相下单、互相担保。前80年，它是人类历史上最成功的商业组织；最后30年，同样的循环结构把它推向崩溃。

关键洞察：循环融资在扩张期是"网络效应的账面表达"，在收缩期就是"多米诺骨牌的物理连接"。同一个结构，两种命运，切换点往往不是基本面而是利率——恰好是华尔希今天在纠结的东西。所以AI叙事和FOMC叙事看似是两条新闻，其实是同一根导火索的两端。

三、令你意外的观察：MAG-7年内已跌5%，而"AI恐慌"是个统计学幻觉

这是全场最被低估的一句话——Gallipo顺口一提：MAG-7年初至今下跌5%，等权重S&P上涨14%，价差近20%。

主流叙事说"AI泡沫撑起了整个市场"。数据说的是完全相反的故事：AI板块正在悄悄失血，而其他499只股票才是牛市的真正引擎。这意味着如果AI真的崩了，指数受到的伤害可能远小于所有人的想象——因为领导权早在几个月前就交接完毕了，只是没人愿意承认。

这里有一个更深的系统性真相：媒体注意力永远滞后于市场领导权的转移。当CNBC还在天天讨论英伟达时，聪明钱已经在买工业股、区域银行、中盘价值股。这就是为什么Gallipo说"过去两年我们最高信念的call"是"离开MAG-7"——他不是在预测未来，他是在读注意力和资金流之间的时间差。

跨领域连接：这和神经科学里的"变化盲视"（change blindness）现象一模一样——大脑锁定在一个显著对象上时，会完全忽视场景中其他更重要的变化。市场也一样。真正的alpha往往藏在你以为不重要的角落，而不是在头条新闻里。

Hi everyone, welcome to another episode of Bits and Bips the Interview. My name is Steve Ehrlich, I'm the head of research at SharpLink and also your host. We've got a terrific show for you today, but as always, before we dive in, just a little bit of housekeeping: nothing that you hear or see on this program is financial or investment advice. For full disclosures, please see unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips.

And now let's briefly pause to hear from one of our sponsors. This episode is brought to you by CAPE, America's privacy-first mobile carrier. Same premium service you'd expect from any other carrier, but designed so your number, your location, and your data actually stay yours. Get 33% off six months at cape.co/unchained.

嘉宾介绍

All right, welcome back. So got a terrific program for you today. A terrific guest — I have Chris Gallipo, he is the head market strategist at Franklin Templeton, at the Franklin Templeton Institute. So welcome, Chris.

— Thank you, Steve. Thanks for having me.

Yeah, got a lot to talk about today. I'm really excited to have you because you're, I guess, a self-described perma-bull. There's a lot of FUD out there — fear, uncertainty, and doubt. I know you're not a crypto native, so maybe you're not up to date on all the lingo, but there's a lot of concern about all the uncertainty in the world: the Iran conflict, oil spiking, tariffs, worries about just like an unending spending spree of CapEx from the MAG-7 and sort of the big AI hyperscalers. And you've been pretty consistent throughout the year that fears of sort of the market topping out are overblown, and we're going to explore all of that today.

But before we do, just really briefly, can you just, for anyone in my audience that doesn't know who you are, explain what you do with the Franklin Templeton Institute?

— Yeah, sure. Happy to. First of all, I am not a perma-bull, just so we're clear on that. We can go into it later, but I do my best to be objective and unbiased. And having spent 25 years as an analyst and PM, you're never perma-anything, right? You're working with the data.

So Franklin Templeton Institute is a part of Franklin Templeton, the asset manager. We run about $2 trillion. The Institute is really the thought leadership part of the organization. So in my role as head strategist, I spend most of my time in the U.S. working with our U.S. clients. So it falls under my purview to build and outline our investment views and opinions, usually for a 12-month window. I will comment on a weekly basis within that 12-month time frame and just try and keep our clients updated on what we see, what we think, what's happening.

This is a great week to be on because there's a lot going on. But you're right — for calendar '26, we've been bullish. We've been right. We could even take it back to longer than that. And I think the themes or the pillars of that argument are still in place. But this will be a great conversation because we can cover everything you just mentioned.

FOMC 与 Kevin Warsh 的首次登场

Yeah. So let's start with the news from yesterday. I mean, it was Kevin Warsh's second meeting chairing the Fed, and my impression from kind of watching at least the beginning of his press conference after the rate announcement — which was basically to hold the whole thing steady for at least another two months — he seemed to be taking a bit of a valedictory victory lap, seeing how rates were going up on their own, the market was deciding, and the Fed didn't have to use forward guidance enough to do all these things. And then he started talking, and the market did not seem to like that. So I'd love to just first get your impressions on sort of how his remarks went and the quick drop and the rise, especially in the 30-year after that happened.

— I think I agree. I generally agree with what you just said, where he spent a lot of time talking about — and this is the second time he's spoken, obviously — he spent a lot of time talking about almost retooling the Fed's kit and pulling in different experts and building these task forces, five of them, to try and evaluate how they assimilate data and make decisions based on the data. So I think that's going to take some time.

But he did talk a lot about, yesterday, the bond market, quote-unquote, doing the work for them. And so I've written about this extensively probably within the past four weeks, every week, where I was having a hard time understanding the movement in two-year yields — two-year note yields, which has a phenomenal long-term track record of predicting Fed policy. The bond market tells the Fed what to do, not the other way around.

And so yesterday, to your point, he said, you know, two-year yields have already moved up. They're 50, 60 basis points above the effective FF rate. That's the bond market telling the Fed you need to raise rates. And that track record is almost perfect.

At the same time, he also referred to the other variable that I watch and that I've written a lot about, which is breakeven rates, which have gone through the floor, collapsed from March. And so that piece of market information is telling us we don't have to worry about inflation. But the two-year note yield is telling us we do, and the Fed should move and not sit tight.

So I found it confusing because on one hand, he's saying, hey, we rely on market-based indicators and the market is the best source of information — which I agree with 100%. But yet the market is telling us this one thing vis-à-vis two-year yields. And I don't necessarily believe that right now.

So the reaction in the bond market was for two-year yields to come in, thinking that, okay, he's probably not going to move here. Well, we didn't think he was going to move yesterday anyway. And he's probably not going to move in September either.

And the 30-year bond, the 30-year guy is saying, "I'm from Missouri. You're talking a big game, prove it, we don't believe it." And so you had the curve steepen on that. Interestingly, 10-year yields really didn't do that much, right? But they're banging around 470, 475 here.

But I think that was the reaction in the bond market. And then you saw the reaction — as soon as he was done talking, it was a straight down move, vortex, in S&P futures. And I think that's the stock market saying, okay, we don't know what to think here. Because he's promoting this lack of forward guidance. And at the same time, he's saying we believe the market-based proxies are the best, that we want to retool while we're going to build the plane while we're flying it. The one thing the stock market doesn't like, Steve, is uncertainty. And they got it yesterday.

Warsh 的两难与美联储独立性

Yeah, I like your analogy of sort of like retooling the plane as we're flying it. Because Kevin Warsh meets — steps in, and I know this is the first time you and I have spoken, but he steps in at a really challenging spot because it's sort of a Rorschach test, reading the economy, reading the labor market, all this macro uncertainty as to what is the right thing to do vis-à-vis rates.

He has to find a way to establish consensus at the FOMC, which is harder now because — I forget, I don't remember exactly how many of the most recent votes have had dissents, but I mean, it's really broken with decades of precedent. And then you have a president who wants us to, quote unquote, have the lowest rates in the world. And Kevin Warsh, he has to navigate all of that.

I don't know if you've ever had a chance to speak with him, if you ever met him. But how do you think he's weighing all those different things? Because clearly he's not getting guidance from the White House. I mean, he understands what the White House wants. And so raising rates would be theoretically problematic from a political point of view. But at the same point in time, there's so many different ways you can read the economy.

And that's what he said yesterday. He was asked directly by one of the reporters in the room, "We've got another inflation data point this morning. How much do you actually believe in this 2% target? Is core PCE your measure?" And he basically said, "Yes, it is, but we're open to evaluating everything and not just going to be reliant on that, although we are anchored to the 2% number."

— Now, so there's a whole host of things and sources of information, market-based and otherwise, that he can look at. I'll give him the benefit of the doubt because I personally am a big believer in the market — or the markets are the collection of intelligence from around the world and different pieces of information. They are always the best reflection of what's known and knowable right now. The dot plot, if you look at that and test it, it has no predictive value. It's not really useful. He's right on that.

As for Trump, I agree with what you said. Warsh has come out and stated, kind of like J-Pow did, we're not going to be swayed by that. We need to be independent. Okay, I get it. I hope that's accurate and true, but I think he is willing, seemingly anyway, to be patient here and see what the data tells us on a go-forward basis and kind of bring in these other groups of what he called, you know, world-class experts to evaluate and go back to first principles. That's his favorite term, right? "Let's go back to first principles and assume that we know nothing and build it up that way."

We'll see how it plays up. But every new Fed chair gets tested, and I think he got tested yesterday. I think there are other things that are going on in the equity market that had really nothing to do with yesterday that we can talk about in a minute.

前瞻指引与市场的不确定性厌恶

Yeah, so I think it's kind of, he — it does seem like they're building the plane while they're flying it, which doesn't seem to be the approach that you want as a market participant, right? Where we want information and we want some sort of — we want to understand the process, we want to understand what sort of data you're using, what's the frequency, what's the source, what can we expect. And he's kind of pulled that away. And that's not easy for markets to digest.

Yeah. And before we move on to some of the other topics that you just alluded to, I want to just double click on sort of his revised, or I guess, yeah, I mean, his new approach to communication, the reduction of forward guidance. I know that it really became a big thing during the great financial crisis, carried on during Powell. And I've said many times on the show that I think part of it is just perhaps maybe Congress abdicating its own responsibility because of just how clouded up it's been from a policy point of view, that the Fed has to become even more ever-present in our lives. But you kind of just hinted on it. Markets don't like uncertainty. So, I mean, he wants to rely on data. He doesn't want to sort of be the Wizard of Oz, like managing things behind the curtain, but it didn't seem to hit the right note yesterday.

— I agree. I mean, I listened to the whole thing and I walked out thinking, "What did he just say? And what should I believe?" And I think that was the general — because then you read the notes, I'm not an economist, you read the notes from the street this morning, even last night after the press conference. And that was the general consensus.

Now, the market might have overreacted a little bit yesterday, shaking it off a little bit now. Look, I'll be honest with you. I'm only interested in what the Fed does if they're starting on a new rate hike cycle or they're about to start a new rate cut cycle. Those are the only real pivot points that I care about. I'm just speaking as an equity guy. I care a lot more about fundamentals — i.e. earnings and earnings season — than I do really anything worse than yesterday. Granted, I stipulated, I thought he was confusing and yesterday was not helpful. I think he's got a heavy lift now to restore his credibility. We'll see how it plays out.

广告插播：CAPE

Okay. All right. Well, we're going to talk about a lot more, but before we do, we have to take one more quick break.
